mandatory_for: EVERY future invention campaign — no exceptions
source_case: OVF-001 (Rounds 34-39): over-drainage prevention via venous-pressure-aware regulation
the_failure_sequence: 1. Problem-first discovery identifies a high-value unmet problem
2. A hydraulic/physical model of the existing system is constructed
3. The model predicts a dangerous phenomenon (e.g., over-drainage)
4. An invention opportunity appears to exist
5. BUT: the model was WRONG (wrong valve type, wrong parameters, inconsistent equations)
6. When the model is corrected (source-bound parameters, consistent equations), the phenomenon disappears
7. The invention opportunity was a MODEL ARTIFACT, not a real problem
mandatory_questions_for_every_new_proble: Q1: Is the model of the existing system source-bound (not assumed)?
Q2: Are the governing equations enforced at every time step (e.g., ΔP = ICP - P_venous)?
Q3: Are INITIAL / TRANSIENT / EQUILIBRIUM phases labeled and not mixed?
Q4: Is the valve/device characteristic curve source-bound from the actual specification (not a single performance point used as a full law)?
Q5: Could this apparent problem disappear because I used the wrong model of the existing system?
Q6: If the model is corrected with source-bound parameters, does the phenomenon still exist?
anti_hallucination_rule: A candidate problem must survive BOTH an existing-system attack AND a model-validity attack before mechanism generation. The model-validity attack asks: 'If I correct the model with source-bound parameters and consistent equations, does the problem still exist?' If the answer is NO, the problem is KILLED_BY_CORRECTED_MODEL — not promoted to mechanism generation.
canonical_lesson: A model can kill a hypothesis inside its domain of validity. It cannot declare reality nonexistent outside that domain. But a WRONG model can CREATE an apparent problem that does not exist. The machine must verify the model before trusting the problem.
